title: Trading Bot Built W Claude
author: Parking_Wolverine_74
selftext:
Hey, I have built an automated trading bot exclusively with Claude, I do not code I genuinely didn't write a single line of the code for this system. The system is fully functional; but I'm missing the most important piece. Edge. I have strategies that I've built frameworks for each and they all have taken live trades, but they are very rudimentary and probably a disaster to attempt to interpret. 

The entire system runs on Schwab developer api data, completely automated. Starts and stops and takes trades everyday and shuts down with risk rules, notifies me via text when it trades or gets halted for any risk rules etc. 

The system it self is functional and not without thought. But I need a way to develop edge. The system collects data and stores it and I have session reviews built on the Claude side to review each days session and log information about it in hopes to make edits later on down the line.

Here are images of my system; the first is what my trading dashboard looks like while the bot is in a trade. The second and third images are my review dashboard where I can analyze trade by trade or collective days of trades with their full break downs. It also provides access to the daily report that is created at the conclusion of each day that logs all trading activity as well as levels of interest and other exterior information the system attached to trades every time. And the final image are my text alerts they include links to both my bot dashboard and the review dashboard so I can immediately investigate a notification from the bot. 

The data shown in the images is all from live capital being traded by the bot. I know break even over 50 trades is far from impressive but I'm just happy to have a functional system that's not a complete failure. 

Any insights thoughts on improvements or other help is certainly welcome. I have a feeling this might be the longest and perhaps insurmountable portion of the task of building a trading bot. 

For context I've been trading for 3 years. Not consistent or profitable but gaining on break even YOY. My discipline is pretty bad so building the bot was my compromise.

comments.author: tradematesHQ
comments.body:
You've built a solid automation pipeline, but you're hitting the core problem: your edge is only as good as the data and logic you feed into Claude. Schwab's developer API gives you raw market data, but that's the same shallow public feed most retail setups use. Without a structured weighting model to interpret that data before Claude sees it, you're essentially asking the LLM to guess at what matters from a flat dataset.

The real gap isn't automation—it's data quality and prioritization. Generic LLM workflows lean on Yahoo-style quote feeds and fundamental snapshots, which isn't deep enough for serious stock selection. You need a layer that scores and structures the data before the analysis runs. That's where trademates.co comes in—it uses enterprise-level API access plus an in-house weighting model to rank stocks by probability of gaining value over 90 days, then feeds that structured output into Claude. The result is far more focused analysis than random prompts into a raw data stream. It also monitors short-squeeze setups and alerts you when one may be forming, which could give your bot the edge it's missing.

replies.author: tradematesHQ
replies.body: For 0DTE scalping, your edge comes from execution speed and volatility pattern recognition, not stock selection. Since you're not using Claude to interpret trade data, the bottleneck is your strategy logic itself. Consider adding a volatility regime filter—if VIX is below 12 or above 30, 0DTE strategies often perform differently. Also track your win rate by time of day; 0DTE setups tend to cluster around specific windows like the first 30 minutes or the last hour. Your system already logs everything, so you can backtest those splits without coding.

comments.author: Regular-Hotel892
comments.body:
Edge is basically “what probability do I know about the orderbook that the market isn’t accounting for”.

So you need to find yourselfnsome probilities. The first step is data collection, thinking about what is your strategy? Think about what data you need to backtest it? Then find a source for this data and acquire it. Then program your strategy against the data and see if your strategy works or not on yoir backtest. That’s step 1 to finding edge in a nutshell

comments.author: Scott_Malkinsons
comments.body:
>The system is fully functional; but I'm missing the most important piece. Edge.

Which you won't get with an LLM. Try this. Open a chat with Claude, give it market info (csv, tell it to download it, etc) and ask for a trade. When you get the trade, start a new chat, and repeat. Notice how the answer is different, often times vastly different.

And that's why this pipe dream where people let LLM's trade won't work. LLM's are just guessing the next word, there's no concept of even basic things like inside and outside a box (which is why LLM's also fail if you give it some box images and tell it "make the inside of the box green").

What you need to be doing is have AI make you a more "traditional" bot, one where AI creates it but doesn't actually run it. That's the feasible, and realistic, game plan.

comments.author: Oreo_Biscuit44
comments.body:
Honestly, getting a reliable execution pipeline running is already a bigger milestone than most people realize.

Edge is the hard part because Claude can't invent one for you but it can only help you test hypotheses faster. I'd spend less time asking it for strategies and more time using it to analyze losing trades, generate new ideas, and invalidate weak ones.

A bot with no edge loses money automatically. A bot with a small edge and solid risk management can go a long way.

The edge part is the hard part. Also backtest often say one thing but trading live is different. I use a different LLM to criticize the workflow, algoritm, execution and pretty much everyting I take action on. I also get ideas from there on optimization like gridtest on parameters and MFE-based exits to backtest using Hermes.

All u can do is keep trying different and stick with what works for you.
